0. FOREWORD
0.1 This Indian Standard (First Revision) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 30 August 1983, after the draft finalized by the Pesticides Residue Analysis Sectional Committee had been approved by the Agricultural and Food Products Division Council. 0.2 BHC ( HCH ) formulations are popular in agriculture and public health for the control of various insect pests and vectors of diseases. Frequent and increased use of these formulations often result in harmful Careful assessment of residues is effects due to toxic nature of residues. therefore, an important step in safeguarding human health and in the establishment of sound regulatory policy. 0.3 This standard was first published in 1971 covering only food grains. The present revision includes other food commodities not covered earlier For and incorporates more sensitive gas chromatographic method. qualitative confirmation of residues, thin layer chromatography has also been prescribed. 0.4 This standard will enable the health authorities uniform test procedure for the estimation of BHC foods. and others to follow residues in various

0.5 In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS : 2 - 1960*.

1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard
prescribes gas chromatographic and spectrophotometric methods for the determination of BHC ( 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6-hexachlorocyclohexane ) residues in foods.
*Rules for rounding off numerical values ( revised).

The operating parameters are set to obtain about half-scale deflection with 1 ng p, p ' -DDE (see 4.3.2 ). Adjust gas flow/column temperature to get adequate resolution of four BHC isomers. Inject standard mixture with the component pesticides (see 4.3.1 ) at three concentration levels with a microlitre syringe. Inject 3-8 ~1 of the cleaned-up sample extract so that the injection volume contains about 400 mg sample equivalents of water and beverages or 20 mg of all other samples. If necessary, dilute the extract suitably so that the peak heights of sample and standards do not vary more than 25 percent. Identify the residues by comparing the retention time of the sample peaks with those of the pesticides standards. 4.5 Calculation BHC residues pg/g ( ppm ) = -x

4.6 Expression of Result - Express BHC residues as the sum alpha-, beta-, gamma- and delta- isomers in the sample as pg/g ( ppm ).

NOTE -Quantify only the peaks which give greater than 10 percent htll-scale deflection ( FSD) when the sample equivalent to 400 mg in the case of water and beverages and 20 mg in the case of others, are injected in CLC. Indicate the compound which produce peaks less than 10 percent FSD as trace (T). If at the retention time of compound, signal is not distinguishable from background, indicate it as not detectable (ND).

4.7 Assuring the Reliability of the Analysis - Pesticide residue analysis involves the determination of the minute quantities of the various compounds in several slrbstrates. Such trace analysis has certain inherent difficulties and the reliability the analytical method should be assured by following the undermentioned procedure. 4.7.1 Take four samples of the size as recommended under 3.3 and fortify three of these at the level of 2.5 ppb in case of water and beverages and 0 03 ppm in the case of other commodities by adding appropriate volume of standard mixture (see 4.3.3 ). Process all the 4 samples following suitable procedure (see 3 and 4 ). The recovery of various residues over the hnckground values obtained from unfortified The sample should be above 80 percent of the added compounds. difference between the recoveries from the fortified replicates should be f 20 percent.
NOTE -If the background values of the residues in the sample are exprctcd IO be high, increase the level of fortification to about double of the expected background lew IS.

5. SPECTROPHOTOMETRIC

METHOD

5.1 Principle - In a specially designed apparatus, BHC is dechlorinated to benzene by the action of zinc and acetic acid in the presence of 12

IS : 6169 - 1983 malonic acid. The carbon dioxide liberated in the process sweeps benzene into the nitrating mixture where it is converted to the dinitrobenzenes which are extracted in ether, evaporated and treated with butanone-2 and alkali to get magenta colour whose absorbance is The amount of BHC in the sample is calculated measured at 565 mm. from the standard curve prepared from lindane ( gamma-BHC ). 5.2 Apparatus

5.4 Preparation of Standard Curve (O-100 ~g Range)Take 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 ml of 20 clg/ml lindane solution inSglacial acetic acid (see 5.3.8.1 ) in reaction flasks of the dechlorinatton apparatus (see Fig. 4 ) and adjust the volume in each flask to IO ml with glacial acetic acid. Add 1 g zinc dust and 2 g malonic acid through a funnel to avoid Attach the condenser and gas their deposition on the glass joint. distribution tubes and seal the joints with acetic acid. Add 10 ml of the Fill the condenser with water but nitrating mixture in the nitration tube. there is no need for the water to flow through it except very warm weather (the idea is to condense the acetic acid but allow benzene vapours to pass into the nitration tube). Reflux vigorously for about three hours. Remove heating and quickly separate the condenser from the reaction flask so as to prevent the nitrating mixture from being sucked back. Using three 20 ml portions of ice cold distilled water, transfer the contents of the nitration tube to a 250 ml separatory funnel. Further rinse the nitration tube into separatory funnel, first with three 20 ml portions of ether and then with three 20 ml of portions of ice cold Shake the separatory funnel for 1 minute and take the distilled water. aqueous layer into another 250 ml separatory funnel and extract it with 20 ml ether. Combine the two ether layers, wash twice with two 20 ml portions of 2 percent sodium hydroxide and then twice with 20 ml Transfer combined ether layer to portions of saturated sodium chloride. a 250 ml Erlenmeyer flask through 1 cm thick layer ofanhydrous sodium sulphate previously washed with ether. Rinse the separatory funnel with 14

two 10 ml portions of ether and add the rinsings to the Erlenmeyer flask through sodium sulphate layer. Add 2 to 3 drops mineral oil and evaporate the ether to about 5 ml on a steam bath and then to dryness at room temperature. Add 10 ml butanone-2 to the flask and swirl it to completely dissolve the residue. Add l ml of 50 percent potassium hydroxide and shake the flask vigorously for one minute. Let the colour develop in the dark for about 15 minutes, decant butanone-2 layer into absorption cell and measure the absorbance at 565 nm against distilled water immediately, as the colour starts fading immediately. Plot absorbance against pg lindane to obtain standard curve. 5.5 Quantitation of BHC in the Samples - Add 2 to 3 drops of mineral oil to the cleaned-up n-hexane extract and concentrate it over a steam bath to about 5 ml. Transfer it to the dechlorination flask with two 3 ml rinsings and let it evaporate to dryness at room temperature. Proceed further as for the preparation of standard curve. If the absorbance is greater than 0.8, dilute suitably with butanone-2 to get a value in the range of 0.2 to 0.8. Calculate BHC in sample using the standard curve. 5.6 Expression as bg/g of the Results Express the residues in the sample

( ppm).

5.7 Assuring the Reliability of the Analysis-Proceed as in 4.7 except that fortify the samples at the level of 0'1 ppm gamma-BHC in the case of water beverages and 1 ppm gamma-BHC in the case of other commodities by adding appropriate volume of standard solution ( see 5.3.8.2 ) and process the samples following the procedures outlined in 3 and 5. 6. CONFIRMATION OF THE RESIDUES

6.0 The identity of the pesticide residues detected and tentatively identified by gas-liquid chromatographic method needs confirmation. Depending on the nature and level of the residues, select one or more of the following confirmatory procedures. 6.1 Alternate GLC Column -The elution pattern of organochlorine insecticide residues on a column packed with 3 percent DEGS on Gas Chrom Q is quite different from other generally used columns. This column may be used for quick confirmation of the low levels of the insecticide residues. -Prepare 0.25 mm thick alumina 6.2 Thin-Layer Chromatography G plates impregnated with about 40 mg silver nitrate per plate. Air dry a plate, activate it at 110�C for 45 minutes and cool it. Spot the insecticide standard mixture ( about 0.05 ml of solution containing 20 beta-, gamma- and delta-BHC isomers in pg/ml of each of the alpha-, hexane ) and suitable aliquots of the cleaned-up extracts. Develop the 15

_,

IS : 6 169 - 1983 plates up to 12 to 15 cm in a saturated chamber, using suitable developing A mixture of n-hexane and benzene solvent, heptane, n-hexane. (4 : 1, v/v) may be used as the developing solvent. Air dry and expose the plate to ultra-violet light for about 30 minutes, when the insecticides residues will appear as black spots. Identify the residues by comparing the RF values with those of the standard co-chromatographed. 6.3 Micro-Alkali Derivatization - Take 5 ml of aliquot of cleaned-up n-hexane extract having residue concentrations suitable for GLC analysis in a 15 ml graduated tube. Add 2 ml ethanolic KOH and heat on a water bath at 50% for 2 hours. Add more n-hexane when the solution in the tube wears drying. Remove the tube from water bath, cool, add 5 ml ethanol : water ( 1 : 1, v/u) and 2 ml hexane, stopper and shake gently. Allow the layers to separate and inject suitable aliquots of of the insecticides n-hexane phase into GLC. C on 6 rm the identity residues by studying the disappearance or shifts in the peak pattern in alkali derivatized sample as compared to underivatized sample. By this treatment, all BHC peaks will completely disappear. 6.4 Interferences due to Polychlorinated Biphenyls - Polychlorinated biphenyls ( PCBS ) are industrial chemicals which are used in manufacture of synthetic rubber, electrical products, printing inks, paints, varnishes, resins, etc. These are resistant to oxidation and reduction and thus, like DDT residues, are widely distributed in the environment. Being polychlorinated biphenyls, these have physical and chemical properties of chlorinated hydrocarbon insecticide residues and thus a method of analysis of DDT and BHC will also detect PCBS. In addition to the environmental contamination of the sample, PCBS from rubber and plastic caps and lining of the containers and laboratory apparatus can also cause interferences. On GLC, PCBS produce multiple peaks some of which may have same retention times as that of BHC and DDT residues. So due care should be taken to avoid the contact of the samples during collection, storage and analysis with rubber or plastics. 6.4.1 If a sample gives multiple peaks on GLC (as will be the case with a sample containing both BHC and DDT residues ), the absence or presence of PCBS can be confirmed by micro-alkali treatment (see 6.3 ). If after the treatment with alkali, the peaks on GLC corresponding to p, p' -DDT p-p ' -DDE and BHC isomers are completely eliminated, it would indicate the absence of PCBs. If there is only partial or no decrease in the peaks heights, sample may be containing PCBS. If the suspected PCBs level is fairly high, their presence can be further confirmed by TLC ( see 6.2 ), when the alkali derivatized sample will give at the most 3 spots (one near the solvent front and two others corresponding to /I, p ' -DDT and DDMU ), rather than giving several spots corresponding to RF values of BHC and DDT residues. i 16
